product.title: Georgian 101 - A1 (English Edition)
product.description: Twenty Assimil-style self-study units that take you from zero to A1 Georgian: the pronunciation printed right above every Mkhedruli word, short dialogues, word-for-word translations that show how Georgian builds its sentences, grammar notes, vocabulary, exercises, and an answer key. Includes a table of all 33 Mkhedruli letters, a guide to the ejective sounds (ყ, ჭ, წ, კ, პ, ტ), the count-in-twenties number system, an A1 verb summary, and a glossary. Each unit targets one of the spots that actually trip English speakers up — from "mama" meaning father to the subject that changes its ending as soon as the story moves into the past.

blocks.text: Georgian is almost always introduced the wrong way. People open the first page, see a row of curls like ღვთისმშობელი, and conclude that the language is beyond ordinary humans. In fact the Mkhedruli alphabet is the **friendliest** part of the whole journey. Thirty-three letters, one letter per sound, without a single exception — no silent letters, no two letters that sound the same, and **no capital letters at all**. If you know the sounds of the thirty-three letters, you can read any Georgian word correctly, including words you've never seen. Compare that with English, where *though*, *through*, *tough*, and *thought* use the same letters for four different sounds.

What's genuinely hard lies in two other places, and this course won't pretend otherwise. First, the **ejectives**. Georgian has a series of consonants made by closing the throat first and then releasing it — კ, პ, ტ, წ, ჭ, ყ — and English has no such sounds. The difference from ordinary k, p, t isn't decoration: კარი (k'ari, door) and ქარი (kari, wind) are two different words. Second, **Georgian verbs pack a huge amount of information into a single word**. მიყვარხარ is one word meaning "I love you" — subject, object, and action all at once. At A1 you don't need to master the whole system, but you do need to know it exists, so you don't try to take it apart the way you'd take apart an English sentence.

The good news: Georgian is **generous** exactly where other languages torture beginners. There's no grammatical gender — no le/la, no der/die/das. There are no articles: სახლი means "house", "a house", and "the house" all at once. Adjectives stand before their noun, as in English, and hardly ever change. And word order is flexible — the subject can go first or last, and the sentence is still correct.

Three things are deliberately done differently from other Georgian textbooks. First, **the pronunciation is printed above each Georgian word**, not on a separate line, so your eyes don't jump back and forth and lose their place mid-sentence. Second, every line of dialogue has a **word-for-word translation** that shows the original order, including when that order sounds strange in English — because that's exactly where the lesson is. Third, every unit targets **one typical mistake English speakers make**, and names it openly instead of hiding it in a footnote.

One last thing. Georgian won't slip into your head through TV series, songs, or social media the way English or Korean might. Four million speakers, one country, one language family unrelated to any major language in the world. Everything you'll have is what you build yourself, page by page. That sounds heavy, but there's an upside: no bad habits to unlearn first, and every word you learn is truly yours. And Georgians reward the effort in a way you rarely find elsewhere — even your first stumbling sentence will be welcomed like good news.

This course has twenty units. Each unit is designed for one sitting — about twenty to thirty minutes — and contains one dialogue, notes on that dialogue, one to three grammar boxes, vocabulary, four exercises, and their answers. If you do one unit a day, you'll finish in three weeks. Three units a week, in seven weeks. Both are fine; what isn't fine is doing five units in one day and then stopping for a month.
The order of work for one unit

items: **Read the dialogue once, only the Georgian script and the pronunciation.** Don't look at the translation. The goal isn't to understand but to get your eyes used to the letter shapes. Say it out loud — Georgian consonant clusters will never get easy if you only read them silently.
**Read it again with the translation and the literal line.** The literal line is the heart of this course. It shows that *თავი მტკივა* really says "head hurts-to-me", not "I have a headache".
**Read the notes.** That's where the trouble spots mentioned in the foreword live.

**Do the exercises without looking back.** Write by hand if you can; writing Mkhedruli by hand forces your brain to take each letter apart, and the curves of ღ, ყ, ჯ only really stick once your own hand has made them.
**Check against the key, then read the dialogue one more time.** The same dialogue will feel different after the exercises.

head: Symbol

rows: Standard Georgian romanization. Vowels are always pure: a as in *father*, e as in *bed*, i as in *machine*, o as in *more*, u as in *rule*. Hyphens separate syllables; a capital letter only marks the start of a sentence or a name.
An **ejective**: k', p', t', ts', ch', q'. Close the throat first, then release. Without the apostrophe it's an ordinary aspirated sound with a puff of air, as in English *kit*, *pot*, *top*.
A word-for-word translation following Georgian order. It often sounds strange — that's the point.

blocks.title: Three ground rules
items: **Don't skip the two alphabet pages and the ejectives page.** The next three pages decide whether your Georgian sounds like Georgian or like English forced into a foreign script.
**Don't memorize the case table at the back yet.** That page is for *checking*, not for *learning*. Noun endings come in through sentences, one at a time, once you need them.
**Say everything out loud.** The difference between კ and ქ, ტ and თ, პ and ფ can't be mastered by eye. Your ears and throat have to do the work.

blocks.text: A small note about the names of the language and country. Georgians call their country **საქართველო** (Sakartvelo) and their language **ქართული** (kartuli) — the word "Georgia" doesn't exist in their own language at all. This course says "Georgian" because that's the name known in English, but from unit 3 on you'll already be calling it by its real name.
Before anything else: the alphabet. This is the one part of the course best finished in a single sitting, because half an hour on this page saves weeks on the pages after it.

The script Georgian uses today is called **მხედრული** (mkhedruli, "the knights' script"). It's one of the few writing systems in the world that stands on its own — not derived from Latin, Arabic, or Indic scripts — and UNESCO has added it to its list of intangible cultural heritage. Two older Georgian scripts, ასომთავრული and ნუსხური, are now used only by the church; you don't need to touch them.
Four things that make it easy

items: **One letter, one sound. Always.** No silent letters, no letter pairs that make a different sound (no "sh", "kh", "ch" to learn as pairs — those sounds have their own letters: შ, ხ, ჩ).
**No capital letters.** Names of people, names of cities, the start of a sentence — all written with the same letters. თბილისი looks exactly the same at the start of a sentence and in the middle.
**No joined letters.** Each letter stands alone, like printed Latin letters. Only quick handwriting joins them, and that's for later.

**There are only five vowels**, and all five are pure: ა a (*father*), ე e (*bed*), ი i (*machine*), ო o (*more*), უ u (*rule*). No long or short vowels, no glides like the "ay" in *day* or the "oh-w" in *go* — ე is always the e of *bed*, ო always a plain o.

blocks.text: Two things that make it feel foreign

items: **Many letters differ by a single curve.** The ones most often mixed up in week one: **ვ** (v) and **კ** (k'), **მ** (m) and **შ** (sh), **ს** (s) and **ხ** (kh), **ბ** (b) and **მ** (m), then **ღ** (gh) and **დ** (d), and **ც** (ts) and **ძ** (dz). There's only one cure: write by hand.

**Some letters rise above or drop below the line**, and that actually helps. ბ, გ, დ, ე drop; ზ, ს, ღ, ყ, ჯ have tails. The silhouette of a Georgian word is very distinctive — after a few days you'll recognize კარგი and მადლობა by their shape before you've even read the letters.

blocks.title: How to learn the alphabet in one hour
items: **Minutes 1–15.** Read the table on the next page once from top to bottom, out loud. Don't memorize, just go through it.
**Minutes 15–35.** Write each letter five times while saying its sound. Five times, not a whole line — what matters is that the sound comes out of your mouth too.

**Minutes 35–50.** Cover the table. Write your own name, your own city, and three everyday English words in Georgian script. *bus* → ბას, *lemon* → ლემონ, *taxi* → ტაქსი. It's fine to get it wrong; what matters is forcing yourself to find the letters.

**Minutes 50–60.** Read the ten words in the "Example" column without looking at the pronunciation. If you get seven out of ten right, you're ready for unit 1. The rest will sort itself out along the way, because every word in this course has its pronunciation above it.

blocks.text: ⚠️ One thing to avoid from day one: **don't learn Georgian through Latin transliteration alone.** The pronunciation in this course is there to help you, not to replace the script. People who stay with transliteration for two months usually give up entirely in the third, because not a single sign, menu, or WhatsApp message in Georgia is written in Latin letters.

The order is the official order of the Georgian alphabet — the same as dictionary order and name lists. The "Say it" column is the symbol used throughout this course. An apostrophe means an **ejective**; the next page is devoted to them.

blocks.title: Six pairs most often mixed up
items: **ვ (v) — კ (k')**: ვ has a single curve to the right, კ has a double curve and a tail going down.
**მ (m) — შ (sh)**: მ has three feet at the bottom, შ rests on one curve.
**ს (s) — ხ (kh)**: ს looks like an upside-down 6, ხ has a small cross in the middle.
**ც (ts) — ძ (dz)**: both curve upward; ძ has an upright stroke that rises higher.
**დ (d) — ღ (gh)**: ღ has a tail hanging below the line, დ doesn't.
**ბ (b) — ბ in clusters**: ბ often sits next to ვ and რ (ბრძოლა), and that's where it's easiest to miss. Read the cluster slowly, letter by letter.

front.title: Ejectives: the one thing that changes everything

blocks.text: Georgian has nine sounds that English doesn't, and six of them belong to one family: **კ, პ, ტ, წ, ჭ, ყ**. They're all made the same way, and once you can do one, the other five follow within minutes.
How to say them

items: Say "ka" as in *car*. Notice the **puff of air** after the k — put your palm in front of your mouth and you'll feel it. That's ქ (k), and English already has it.
Now hold your breath. Close your throat as if you were about to lift something heavy, then say "ka" **without letting any air out** — the sound becomes shorter, tighter, as if tapped. That's კ (k').
Repeat with p: ფ (p, aspirated) versus პ (p', ejective). Then t: თ (t) versus ტ (t'). Then ts: ც (ts) versus წ (ts'). Then ch: ჩ (ch) versus ჭ (ch').

blocks.text: ⚠️ This isn't a matter of accent. An aspirated sound and an ejective are **two different letters**, and the difference changes the meaning of the word:

If you ask for ფური instead of პური at the bakery, the baker will laugh — but will still understand from where they're standing. A wrong ejective will **not** stop a conversation. What matters is that you know the difference exists and you're aiming for it; perfection comes later.
The remaining three sounds

items: **ყ (q')** — the most feared. Not "k" and not "kh": the throat closes **deeper** than for კ, almost at the root of the tongue, then releases. It's in words you'll use every day: ყავა (q'ava, coffee), წყალი (ts'q'ali, water), ყველი (q'veli, cheese). For now, say it as a very deep, short "k"; people will understand.

**ღ (gh)** — this sound exists in Arabic (غ) and is close to the French r. Like g, but not tapped — **rubbed** continuously at the back of the throat. Practice: say "kh" (as in *loch*), then add your voice without moving your mouth. Practice words: ღვინო (ghvino, wine), მაღაზია (maghazia, shop).
**ხ (kh)** — the voiceless partner of ღ, and actually easy: exactly the ch of Scottish *loch* or German *Bach*. Practice words: ხაჭაპური, ხინკალი, ოთხი.

blocks.title: About consonant clusters — and stress
items: Georgian lets consonants pile up with no vowel in between. მწვრთნელი (mts'vrtneli, coach) has six consonants in a row, and it's an ordinary word used in sports broadcasts. You won't meet anything that extreme in this course, but ვ, რ, ლ, მ, ნ really do often attach straight onto other consonants: მთა (mta, mountain), ცხრა (tskhra, nine), ბრძოლა (brdzola, struggle).
The way out is not to insert a vowel. Don't read მთა as "mata" or "muta" — that becomes another word. Read the m and t **together**, like saying "hmm-ta" without the hmm.

**Word stress in Georgian is weak and almost never changes meaning.** That's a big relief compared to Russian or English: you don't need to memorize the stress of a single word. Roughly, two-syllable words are stressed on the first syllable (**k'ar**gi, **de**da), longer words on the third syllable from the end (ga**mar**joba). If in doubt, say it evenly — that actually sounds more Georgian than stressing too hard.

back.title: Noun endings: six forms on two pages

blocks.text: This page is for **checking**, not for learning up front. Every form below has already appeared one by one in the units, in sentences that had a reason to use it. If a row feels unfamiliar, go back to the unit given in the last column.

Georgian nouns change their ending according to their role in the sentence. The dictionary form (the one in the vocabulary lists) always ends in **-ი** or a vowel. Only the ending changes; the body of the word stays the same.

blocks.title: Three things that save a lot of memorizing
items: **The -ი ending drops before another ending.** სახლი → სახლ**ს**, სახლ**ის**, სახლ**ში**. Never write სახლის**ი**.
**Postpositions attach to the object or possessive form**, written as one word: სახლ**ში** (at home), მაგიდა**ზე** (on the table), ექიმ**თან** (at the doctor's), თბილისი**დან** (from Tbilisi).
**Adjectives change too, but lazily.** დიდი სახლი → დიდ სახლში (in the big house): the adjective's -ი drops, and that's it. At A1 you can stop there.

blocks.text: ⚠️ Nouns ending in **-ა** and **-ო** (მამა, ბიჭო, რადიო) behave slightly differently: their dictionary form doesn't end in -ი, so nothing drops. მამა → მამა**ს**, მამა**ს**თან. These are called vowel-stem nouns, and there aren't many of them.

back.title: A1 verb forms at a glance

blocks.text: Georgian verbs carry their subject inside the word, so მე (I), შენ (you), ის (he/she) can actually be dropped. All you must recognize are the subject markers.
Subject markers in the present
The core verbs that cover almost all of A1
Inverted verbs: the person comes in as a prefix

A group of important verbs makes **the thing** the grammatical subject, while the person comes in as a მ-/გ-/ს- prefix. All of them have already appeared in units 4, 10, and 16 — they're just collected here.
Just enough past and future

blocks.title: Two guardrails that rescue a lot of sentences
items: **In the past, the subject changes its ending to -მა.** დედა**მ** თქვა (mother said), ანი**მ** იყიდა (Ani bought). This only applies to verbs that have an object — not to წავედი, მოვედი, ვიყავი. See unit 17.

**The future is often just the present + a prefix.** ვჭამ → **შე**ვჭამ, ვწერ → **და**ვწერ, ვხედავ → ვნახავ. The prefix can't be guessed and has to be learned verb by verb — but at A1, the ten verbs in the table above cover almost every conversation.

blocks.text: Georgian numbers count **in twenties**, not tens. French does the same (quatre-vingts), and so does Danish, and once you see the pattern, the first ninety-nine numbers fall out of just ten words.

items: **11–19 are formed from the unit number + -მეტი** ("more"): ცამეტი 13 = a changed სამი (3) + მეტი. No need to take them apart; just learn these ten words as they are.
**20, 40, 60, 80 are multiples of twenty**: ოცი (20), ორმოცი (2×20), სამოცი (3×20), ოთხმოცი (4×20).
**Numbers in between = the multiple + და + the rest**: ოცდაერთი 21 (20 and 1), ორმოცდახუთი 45 (40 and 5), სამოცდაცხრამეტი 79 (60 and 19).
**Hundreds and thousands are straightforward**: ორასი 200, ხუთასი 500, ორი ათასი 2,000, ორი ათას ოცდახუთი 2,025.
⚠️ **Nouns after numbers stay singular.** ორი ძმა (two brother), not ორი ძმები. A relief, not a trap — unlike English, there's no plural to add.

blocks.text: Telling the time

⚠️ **ხუთის ნახევარი means 4:30, not 5:30.** Georgian counts the half *toward* the next hour, as Dutch and German do — the opposite of British "half five". This is the most common cause of learners arriving an hour late in Tbilisi.
Days and months

blocks.title: Saying the date
items: **რიცხვი** (ritskhvi) = date. *დღეს ხუთი მაისია* — today is May 5.
What's the date? — **რა რიცხვია დღეს?** (ra ritskhvia dghes)
Year: **წელი** (ts'eli). *ორი ათას ოცდახუთი წელი* — the year 2025.
Yesterday — **გუშინ** (gushin) · today — **დღეს** (dghes) · tomorrow — **ხვალ** (khval) · the day after tomorrow — **ზეგ** (zeg)

blocks.text: ⚠️ **თქვენ is used for two things at once**: "you" (several people) and polite "you" (one person, formal). With older people, shopkeepers, doctors, or anyone you've just met — use თქვენ. With peers after a few minutes of chatting, შენ. Georgians usually offer it first: *შეიძლება "შენ"?*

blocks.text: Thirty words that bring sentences to life
The most-searched-for words, in English alphabetical order. The pronunciation is shortened; an apostrophe still marks an ejective.

If you've reached this page after working through all twenty units, your vocabulary is around five hundred words and you can: introduce yourself, ask and say where people are from, talk about family, order at a café and a restaurant, bargain at the market, ask for directions, tell the time and the day, describe your daily routine, talk about the weather, use public transport, shop for clothes, make plans, explain your symptoms to a doctor, and tell a story about something that's already happened. That's a full A1, and more than enough for two weeks in Georgia without relying on English.
Four things to do next

items: **Reread this course from unit 1, without looking at the pronunciation.** Cover the transliteration line with paper. What once took half a minute per line will now flow, and that's the most honest measure of progress.

**Move on to the past and future seriously.** Units 17 and 18 only open the door. The full system — what Georgians themselves call *სერიები* (series) — is A2 work, and that's where Georgian turns from "memorized sentences" into a language you can tell stories in.
**Collect inverted verbs.** მაქვს, მინდა, მიყვარს, მომწონს, მესმის, მტკივა — the group is small but used constantly, and there's no other language you can lean on to guess them.

**Write five sentences a day in Georgian script.** Not five paragraphs — five sentences. About anything: the weather, lunch, tomorrow's plans. What stops people at A1 is almost never a lack of material, but a habit that stops.

blocks.title: Materials that genuinely help after this course
items: **Songs.** Georgian polyphonic music (ჩაკრულო, შენ ხარ ვენახი) is sung slowly with repetitive lyrics — the best listening material for beginners. For something lighter, find modern Georgian pop songs and read the lyrics as you listen.

**Signs and menus.** If you're in Tbilisi, read everything that's written: მაღაზია, აფთიაქი, გასასვლელი (exit), შესვლა (entrance). Reading the script in the real world sticks much faster than reading word lists.
**One native speaker, once a week.** Georgians are almost always willing. You've had the opening line since unit 1: *გამარჯობა, მე ქართულს ვსწავლობ.*
**Linguo Private Classes.** This course lays the foundation; what no book can give you is the person across the table who stops you when your ყ sounds like კ. linguo.id

blocks.text: **გისურვებთ წარმატებას!** (gisurvebt ts'armat'ebas) — good luck. And if you ever find yourself at a supra and someone raises a glass toward you, one word is enough: **გაუმარჯოს!**
